A cold can. A station bento. A changing view.
Discover everyday Japanese beer on Japan’s bullet train.
Find a beer for your journey
A SMALL PLEASURE OF THE JOURNEY
Make the ride part of the holiday.

You have bought a station bento, found your seat and put your bags away. Outside, the city gives way to fields. A beer can be a small way to settle into the journey — and to get a taste of daily life in Japan.

Beer became part of modern Japan as breweries grew in the late 1800s, from Yokohama to Hokkaido. Today, you can begin with an ordinary cold can. Learn what makes it interesting, then look outside: Kirin and Sapporo have breweries beside the Tokaido Shinkansen.
Can you drink beer on the Shinkansen?
Yes. Food and drinks are welcome at your seat; enjoy them quietly and be considerate of other passengers. Buy before boarding an ordinary car on the Tokaido Shinkansen.
Golden lagers, with different ideas of refreshment.
The familiar cans from Kirin, Asahi, Sapporo and Suntory are a good place to begin. Here is what to notice beyond the name.
What makes the everyday beer distinctive?

Japan’s big breweries are especially associated with pilsner-style lagers: golden beers with a refreshing character that sits easily beside food. That is a useful starting point, rather than a description of every beer made in Japan.

Within this family, small differences matter. Malt gives grain-like flavour and body; hops contribute bitterness and aroma. A “dry” finish fades quickly, while a fuller beer may leave more flavour after the sip. These are clues you can enjoy with a bento, without needing a tasting vocabulary.
Begin with the kind of finish you like. The four cans below offer different approaches to malt, aroma and refreshment. Their tasting prompts are invitations to notice something for yourself.
Is Japanese beer always rice beer?

Some familiar lagers include rice, but the recipes differ. In Japan, Super Dry and Black Label list rice, corn and starch alongside malt and hops. Ichiban Shibori and the classic Premium Malt’s are all-malt beers.
“Japanese” tells you where the beer tradition comes from; it does not give you one recipe. The can’s ingredients tell you more.

“Ichiban shibori” means first pressing. Kirin uses only the first wort — the liquid drawn from the malt mash before fermentation — for this all-malt beer. The name describes a brewing choice, not a beer style.
If malt flavour appeals to you, start here. Take a sip before your first bite and notice the grain-like character.
Look for the big 一番搾り lettering and Kirin’s mythical creature.
Meet Kirin again beside the tracks

Launched in 1987, Super Dry made a crisp finish its signature. Asahi calls this character “karakuchi”: flavour that arrives clearly, then finishes quickly. The word 辛口 on a beer label does not mean chilli heat.
If you prefer a brisk finish, start here. Notice how much flavour remains after a sip, then try it beside a savoury bite.
Look for the silver can, Asahi lettering and 辛口 (karakuchi).

Black Label puts malt flavour and a refreshing aftertaste together. It is a useful middle ground to explore when you want some body as well as a clean finish. Despite the name, the beer in this can is a golden lager.
For a bento with several little dishes, try noticing how the same sip feels after each different bite.
Look for SAPPORO, a gold star and the dark circular label.

Suntory gives this all-malt lager a fuller flavour and a fragrant hop aroma. Malt is heated in two boiling steps, while European aroma hops supply another part of its character. The classic beer belongs to a wider family that also includes ales.
If aroma interests you, pause before the first sip and take in the scent. A familiar lager can have plenty to explore.
Look for The PREMIUM MALT’S. You may also hear its Japanese nickname, プレモル (Premol).
Your ekiben is a little tasting companion.

is a bento sold for a train journey, often with a local theme. Try a sip on its own, then another after a bite of grilled fish, fried chicken or soy-seasoned vegetables. Does the malt stand out, or does the finish feel more refreshing?
Choose a beer for one leg of your trip and a different flavour another day. A town passing the window, the bento’s regional name and the can on your table can become one small memory of the journey.
A little help with the label.
The maker’s name, the beer style and words such as “nama” tell you different things. Here is enough to make the next can more interesting.
Lagers and ales use different yeasts and fermentation conditions. Many familiar Japanese golden beers are lagers.
Ales are generally fermented at warmer temperatures. They often offer fruity or expressive aromas, though both families cover a wide range of flavours.
A name to try: Kaoru Ale
. The ale in the Premium Malt’s family is another direction to explore. Suntory describes a fruity aroma and a refreshing finish — look for the extra words beside the family name.
describes the colour, with dark malts often adding toasted or roasted notes. A dark beer can be a lager or an ale.
is not one flavour or a fermentation method. There is no single agreed definition in Japan; look for the beer’s style and the maker’s description.

“Dry” describes the beer’s crisp character, not chilli heat.

03 / FROM THE CAN TO THE LANDSCAPE
The beer on your table has a place in the view.
On the Tokaido Shinkansen between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka, a name you have just learned can appear beside the tracks. Two breweries turn the station shelf into a story about the places you are passing.
Kirin, on a much bigger scale.
Look for the rows of silver tanks at Kirin’s Nagoya brewery, between Nagoya and Gifu-Hashima. The name from the can has become a place beside the tracks.
You do not need to know the brewing equipment to enjoy the connection. Recognising KIRIN is enough to give this stretch of the journey a small new story.

The Sapporo name may make you think of Hokkaido, Japan’s northern island. These large tanks are in Yaizu, at Sapporo’s Shizuoka brewery, between Shizuoka and Kakegawa.
A beer brand can take you beyond the city in its name. From the A-seat side, the tanks become a brief landmark in the landscape.

A and E refer to the window-seat sides of ordinary cars on the Tokaido Shinkansen. These views connect a brand with its brewery; they do not identify where your particular can was made.

Allow time to choose your bento and drink. Common can sizes are 350 ml and 500 ml; check the volume and alcohol percentage on the can. These four brands are useful names to look for, while stock and packaging vary by shop.
On the Tokaido Shinkansen, ordinary cars have no onboard sales. Nozomi and Hikari Green cars have a mobile-order service; check its current menu and availability.
Get settled before opening the can, use the tray table and keep your voice down. Put empty cans and food packaging in the appropriate bins or take them with you.

fr.6: Une canette fraîche. Un bento. Un paysage qui défile.
fr.7: Découvrez les bières du quotidien à bord du train à grande vitesse japonais.
fr.8: Trouver une bière pour le trajet
fr.11: Le trajet fait aussi partie des vacances.
fr.12: Bento acheté, place trouvée, bagages rangés : la ville cède aux champs. Une bière peut aider à entrer dans le voyage et à goûter au quotidien japonais.
fr.13: À la fin du XIXe siècle, les brasseries de Yokohama à Hokkaido ont ancré la bière dans le Japon moderne. Commencez par une canette fraîche, puis regardez dehors : Kirin et Sapporo ont des brasseries près du Tokaido Shinkansen.
fr.14: Peut-on boire une bière dans le Shinkansen ?
fr.15: Oui, à votre place, tranquillement et avec égard pour les autres. Achetez avant de monter en voiture ordinaire du Tokaido Shinkansen.
fr.24: Des lagers dorées, plusieurs façons de rafraîchir.
fr.25: Les canettes Kirin, Asahi, Sapporo et Suntory offrent un point de départ. Voici quoi observer au-delà du nom.
fr.27: Les grandes brasseries japonaises sont associées aux lagers de type pilsner : dorées, rafraîchissantes et adaptées aux repas. Un point de départ, pas une description de toutes les bières japonaises.
fr.28: Le malt apporte céréales et corps, le houblon amertume et parfum. Une finale « dry » s’efface vite ; une bière ample persiste davantage. Avec un bento, nul besoin de vocabulaire expert pour observer ces différences.
fr.29: Partez de la finale que vous aimez. Ces quatre canettes explorent malt, arôme et fraîcheur ; les pistes de dégustation invitent à observer par vous-même.
fr.30: La bière japonaise est-elle toujours au riz ?
fr.31: Les recettes varient. Au Japon, Super Dry et Black Label contiennent riz, maïs et amidon, en plus du malt et du houblon. Ichiban Shibori et Premium Malt’s classique sont pur malt.
fr.32: « Japonaise » situe une tradition, pas une recette unique. Lisez les ingrédients.
fr.39: « Ichiban shibori » signifie premier pressage. Kirin n’utilise que le premier moût issu du brassin avant fermentation pour cette bière pur malt. Le nom désigne un choix de brassage, pas un style.
fr.41: Si le malt vous attire, commencez ici. Avant la première bouchée, prenez une gorgée et observez les notes céréalières.

fr.48: Lancée en 1987, Super Dry se distingue par sa finale nette. Asahi la nomme « karakuchi » : un goût franc qui s’efface vite. 辛口 ne signifie pas piquant comme le piment.
fr.49: Pour une finale vive, observez ce qui reste après une gorgée, puis essayez avec une bouchée salée.
